standard.title: The Australian Legal System
standard.description: the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Australian Constitution, the rule of law and the court system
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand that Australia's Constitution established the framework of government (AC9HC7K01). They know about democratic values including fairness and equality from primary HASS (AC9HS6K06). This is the first systematic treatment of Australia's legal system as a distinct institution.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Constitution, the rule of law, principles of justice and the court hierarchy.

nodes.label: Origins of Australia's legal system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the origins of Australia's legal system, including British common law, the Magna Carta, and the establishment of an independent judiciary.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that Australia's legal system is based on British common law and explain the key principle inherited from the Magna Carta that no person is above the law.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the origins of Australia's legal system in British common law and the Magna Carta; describe the role of an independent judiciary in applying the law impartially; identify the federal and state/territory court hierarchies.
wider: Investigate the historical significance of the Magna Carta (1215) and trace how its principles of limiting government power and protecting individual rights developed into modern Australian law
Explore how Australian common law has developed differently from UK law since 1901, including landmark cases that changed Australian law
Examine the concept of legal precedent (stare decisis) and how decisions made in higher courts bind lower courts
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of common law and its basis in precedent is foundational for understanding how Australian law develops and why court hierarchy matters. Students who don't grasp the origin story will treat the court system as arbitrary bureaucracy rather than a principled institution.

response_modes.reason: The idea that law can be 'made' through judicial decisions (common law) rather than only through legislation is genuinely novel — invest in the reasoning scaffold that shows how precedent accumulates into binding legal principles.

success_criteria: Identify that Australia's legal system is based on British common law
Explain the key principle that no person is above the law and trace its origins to the Magna Carta

nodes.label: Rule of law and principles of justice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the rule of law and the principles of justice, fairness, equality, presumption of innocence, burden of proof, and the right to a fair trial.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the rule of law (that everyone is subject to the same law, applied equally) and identify at least two principles of a fair legal system (e.g. presumption of innocence, right to a fair trial).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the rule of law and its relationship to democratic principles; describe the principles of justice, fairness, equality, presumption of innocence, burden of proof, and the right to a fair trial and legal representation; make connections between these principles and democratic values.
wider: Investigate examples where the rule of law has been challenged in Australia, such as cases involving the legality of government actions, and examine how the courts resolved them
Examine how the principle of equal access to justice operates in practice through legal aid, community legal centres, and self-represented litigants
Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have experienced the Australian legal system, including historical inequalities in the application of law
nodes.hinge_reason: The rule of law and fair trial principles are the conceptual core of the legal system. Without understanding these, students cannot assess whether a legal system is working as intended or evaluate proposed reforms. The concepts in K04 and K05 (social cohesion, democratic values) rely on students grasping why impartial law matters.

response_modes.reason: The rule of law needs careful unpacking — students need to understand why equal application of law is a principled achievement, not a given, and what happens when it fails.

First Nations Australians' historical experience of unequal application of law provides concrete context for understanding why rule of law principles matter and what is at stake when they are not upheld.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australians' experience with the legal system — including Protection Acts, stolen generations, and over-representation in the justice system — makes the rule of law and equal access to justice genuinely meaningful topics with real-world stakes.
success_criteria: Explain the rule of law and what it means for how law is applied in Australia
Identify at least two principles of a fair legal system (e.g. presumption of innocence, burden of proof) and explain why each matters

nodes.label: Court hierarchy and fair trial
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe Australia's court hierarchy (federal and state/territory) and explain the elements of a fair trial, including the roles of witnesses, jurors, legal representation, and due process.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that Australia has a hierarchy of courts (magistrates, district/county, supreme, and federal) and explain at least two elements of a fair trial (e.g. legal representation, role of jurors).
nodes.typical_width: Describe the federal and state/territory court hierarchies; explain the elements of a fair trial including the roles of citizens as witnesses and jurors, legal representation, due process, and the significance of an independent judiciary.
wider: Investigate how a case moves through the court hierarchy (from lower to higher courts on appeal) using a real or hypothetical case
Explore how legal aid and community legal services provide access to justice for people who cannot afford legal representation
Examine the role of the jury system in Australian democracy — why citizens are asked to make legal judgments and what obligations this creates

response_modes.reason: Tracing a case through the court hierarchy using a concrete example is more effective than describing the hierarchy in the abstract — the procedural logic becomes clearer when students see it in motion.

success_criteria: Identify at least three levels of the Australian court hierarchy and describe the role of each
Explain two elements of a fair trial and why each is important to a just legal system

nodes.label: Legal system and democratic principles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the connections between a fair and just legal system and democratic principles, and understand how access to justice is supported in Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one connection between the rule of law and democratic principles (e.g. legal equality supports democratic equality) and identify that legal aid exists to support access to justice.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how a fair and just legal system supports democracy by enforcing rights, constraining government power, and providing mechanisms for resolving disputes; describe how Australians can access justice including through legal aid and legal representation.
wider: Investigate a reform to the Australian legal system that aimed to improve access to justice or equality before the law, and evaluate whether it achieved its goals
Explore how the legal system interacts with democratic rights — for example, how the right to protest is protected and how courts have interpreted free speech cases
Compare access to justice across different groups in Australia (e.g. by socioeconomic status, location, cultural background) and identify systemic barriers

response_modes.reason: This node synthesises the constitutional foundation, rule of law, and court system into a coherent picture of how the legal system serves democratic values — it is the point where the building blocks connect.

success_criteria: Explain at least one connection between a fair legal system and democratic principles
Describe how citizens can access legal representation and justice in Australia
